The fracture was not a classical soft tissue Chance fracture, as it disrupted the posterior elements at T7/8, and the intervertebral disc at the level below (Figure 1). There was, therefore, some bony involvement, with the fracture passing through the lamina of T8 (Figure 3). A: Radiograph documenting severe deformity (36° Cobb angle) resulting from a pediatric Chance fracture, which is the primary condition discussed in the case report. B: Lateral radiograph documenting the kyphosis angle (31 degrees) associated with the underlying Chance fracture complication. C: AP radiograph showing coronal deformity (30mm shift) related to the skeletal instability caused by the Chance fracture. D: Lateral radiograph documenting the successful reduction of the kyphotic angle (to 2.4°) post-correction procedure for the Chance fracture complication.

panels.figure_caption: T2-weighted MRI demonstrating T8 chance fracture with associated thoracic duct rupture (black arrows) and ductal duplication (green arrows). Panels A-C represent three contiguous coronal T2-weighted slices arranged from anterior (A) to posterior (C). Black arrows indicate disruption of the thoracic duct, and green arrows demonstrate duplicated thoracic ducts present on both sides of the spine. A right-sided pleural effusion is present in all panels. The thoracic duct rupture and duplication are most clearly visualized in panel B. Images were obtained on a 3.0-T MRI scanner with fat suppression.
in_text_mentions: place a pigtail catheter and attach it to suction, yielding 1,800 mL of serosanguinous fluid. On hospital day three, it was noted that the fluid in the pleur-evac was topped by a milky white layer, which raised suspicion for chylothorax. The fluid was analyzed and was positive for chylomicrons and yielded a triglyceride level of 798 mg/dL, which exceeds the diagnostic standard of 110 mg/dL for chylothorax. The patient was sent for an MRI to evaluate for potential sources of the leak. A right-sided thoracic duct rupture was discovered, just lateral to the site of the spinal fracture (Figure 1).
